site.name: lumen-research
site.summary: Lumen Research — research assistant (local demo) Fictional research-assistant chat product. Local fixture for UXBench. Open `index.html` directly. Page `index.html` — Research thread Three-column layout: left rail for thread history, center conversation, right rail for Sources. Center column: - Conversation styled with serif body type. Each assistant turn renders inline citations as small chips (`[1]`, `[2]` …). Hovering a citation highlights and scrolls the matching source on the right; clicking jumps to it. - Embedded tables and lists are styled with the rest of the conversation.

run_plan.goal: Critique and validate the end-to-end UX of the Lumen Research research-assistant chat interface, including citation-source navigation, thread management, export/share, mode controls, and mobile usability.
run_plan.summary: Start by exercising the primary chat thread flow on index.html: interact with existing thread topics, use the follow-up input, and validate citation-chip behavior with the Sources rail (hover highlight + click jump). Then test adjacent controls in the header/footer—mode selector, sort, filter tabs, share thread, export as PDF, and the attachment icon—followed by stress tests using the three 'button prompts' shown in the message (find papers/power analysis/negative results). Finish by repeating critical actions on a mobile viewport and verifying tap target and label/aria issues.
assumptions: The only known HTML page is index.html; all interactions occur within this single-page UI (no other pages are discoverable from the prescan).
Citation chips in assistant messages should map to items in the right Sources panel, with hover highlighting/scrolling and click navigation/jump behavior.
Header controls (Mode select, Share thread, Export as PDF, + New thread, 📎) operate in-place without full page navigation.
risk_hotspots: index.html: citation-chip hover vs click synchronization with the Sources rail (risk of wrong mapping, lack of scroll, or missing highlight)
index.html: Mode selector (Balanced/Quick scan/Deep dive/Compare arguments) and whether it changes output + affects source handling
index.html: Sort selector in Sources (Relevance/Date/Cited in this answer) and Sources tab set (All/Papers/Books/Web/Preprints) possibly not updating content reliably
index.html: Export as PDF and Share thread flows (risk of blocked downloads, missing permissions, or silent failures)
index.html: attachment/📎 button behavior (risk of missing file-picker, wrong affordance, or errors)
index.html: follow-up textarea labeled via placeholder only (risk of missing accessible label/keyboard focus issues)
index.html: mobile tap targets flagged as small (e.g., + New thread 215x42; many topic links 215x38; mode control and source tabs), plus missing input label on Mode select noted by prescan

phases.title: Baseline walkthrough of the primary chat experience
phases.objective: Validate that the existing conversation renders correctly and that core interactions (topic selection + follow-up) produce coherent updates.
key_checks: Click one topic link in the left thread history (e.g., 'Deep work scheduling literature') and confirm the center conversation updates or scrolls to the associated thread content.
Use the follow-up textarea: type a short question referencing the current answer (e.g., ask for study design notes or effect-size interpretation) and press Ask.
Observe whether the assistant response includes inline citation chips and whether any new Sources items appear/expand in the right rail.
exit_criteria: At least one left-rail topic click demonstrably changes the displayed conversation state (scroll or content update).
A follow-up submission produces a new assistant turn with citation chips present in the conversation.
Sources rail updates to include/reflect the citations used in the new assistant turn.

phases.title: Citation-to-source navigation (hover + click) validation
phases.objective: Ensure citations in the chat map accurately to entries in Sources and that the interaction model is consistent and discoverable.
key_checks: Hover over multiple citation chips in the assistant message and verify the corresponding source item highlights and scrolls into view in the Sources rail.
Click a citation chip and confirm it jumps to the matching source entry (and that the page focus/scroll position updates appropriately).
Change Sources sort and repeat one citation interaction to confirm mapping remains correct regardless of ordering.
If possible, test a citation chip when the source is not currently visible without scrolling (confirm the UI still navigates correctly).
exit_criteria: Hover and click both reliably identify the correct source item for at least 3 different citations.
Citation navigation continues to work after changing Sources sort (Relevance/Date/Cited in this answer).

phases.title: Mode control + compare/assist actions
phases.objective: Validate that the Mode selector meaningfully changes agent behavior and that downstream UI elements (sources, sorting, citations) remain functional.
key_checks: Use the Mode select (Balanced, Quick scan, Deep dive, Compare arguments) to trigger a mode change and then ask a short follow-up question.
Specifically choose 'Quick scan' and re-ask the same or similar question to check output verbosity/format changes (e.g., shorter bullets vs detailed response).
Choose 'Compare arguments' and ask a comparison-focused question; verify response includes appropriate structure and citations.

Use the existing message buttons (if they are actionable prompts): 'Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules', 'Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks', and 'Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help'—execute at least 2 and confirm assistant responses reflect the intent.
exit_criteria: At least 3 mode selections produce meaningfully different assistant output characteristics.
At least 2 of the visible prompt buttons generate agent responses that align with their described tasks.

phases.title: Share/export/attachment + accessibility risk checks
phases.objective: Validate non-chat utility controls (share/export/attachment) and verify critical accessibility concerns (labels, focus, keyboard behavior).
key_checks: Click 'Share thread' and confirm expected share behavior (e.g., dialog/link generation) or graceful failure messaging.
Click 'Export as PDF' and verify a PDF download/render occurs without blank/partial content.
Click the 📎 attachment button to confirm whether a file picker/open action appears; attempt cancelling if no file is selected.
Verify keyboard navigation: Tab to the follow-up textarea and Ask button; submit with Enter (if supported).
Check select control accessibility: ensure Mode select has an accessible name/label (prescan flagged missing input label for select).
exit_criteria: Share thread either produces a usable share link/dialog or shows clear error/disabled state (no silent no-op).
Export as PDF completes with a plausible, content-inclusive PDF (or provides clear error).
Attachment control responds with a visible UI for file selection or a clear explanation.

phases.title: Mobile viewport repeat of critical flows
phases.objective: Re-validate primary interactions under mobile constraints and address tap-target and layout risks flagged by prescan.
key_checks: Repeat: topic link click (1), follow-up Ask (1), citation hover/click navigation (2 citations).
Repeat mode change + one assistant question.
Attempt Source rail interactions: change Sort selector once and click a Sources tab (All/Papers/Books/Web/Preprints) if available on mobile layout.
Observe tap target effectiveness for + New thread and left topic links (many flagged as <44px height/width).
exit_criteria: All critical actions succeed on mobile: selecting a topic, submitting a follow-up, and navigating citations to sources.
No critical controls become unreachable/overlaid; any interaction failures are clearly explained to the user.

coverage_targets.pages: Visit all known HTML pages (index.html only).
coverage_targets.features: Exercise most visible controls per key page: + New thread, left topic links, follow-up textarea + Ask, Mode selector, Share thread, Export as PDF, 📎 attachment, Sources sort and tabs, and at least 2 of the three assistant prompt buttons shown.
coverage_targets.mobile: Repeat critical checks on mobile viewport: topic selection, follow-up submission, citation navigation, mode switch, and one Sources interaction (sort or tab).

notes: No navigation to other HTML pages is expected; treat this run as a single-page interaction audit focused on state transitions within index.html.
Prioritize evidence quality for citation mapping and export/share outcomes; these are high-risk for UX regressions and user trust.

observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertnes

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertnes

observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you propose a concrete study design (randomization, sample size considerations, and outcomes) to test the two-morning-90-minute-blocks vs afternoon-heavy schedule comparison? Please include citations for key assumptions. L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you propose a concrete study design (randomization, sample size considerations, and outcomes) to test the two-morning-90-minute-blocks vs afternoon-heavy schedule comparison? Please include citations for key assumptions. L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-u

observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you propose a concrete study design (randomization, sample size considerations, and outcomes) to test the two-morning-90-minute-blocks vs afternoon-heavy schedule comparison? Please include citations for key assumptions. L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. I added 3 new sources to the panel on the right. Want me to dig into any of them in particular? 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-u

observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you propose a concrete study design (randomization, sample size considerations, and outcomes) to test the two-morning-90-minute-blocks vs afternoon-heavy schedule comparison? Please include citations for key assumptions. L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you propose a concrete study design (randomization, sample size considerations, and outcomes) to test the two-morning-90-minute-blocks vs afternoon-heavy schedule comparison? Please include citations for key assumptions. L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you propose a concrete study design (randomization, sample size considerations, and outcomes) to test the two-morning-90-minute-blocks vs afternoon-heavy schedule comparison? Please include citations for key assumptions. L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you propose a concrete study design (randomization, sample size considerations, and outcomes) to test the two-morning-90-minute-blocks vs afternoon-heavy schedule comparison? Please include citations for key assumptions. L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.title: Lumen Research — research assistant
observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you propose a concrete study design (randomization, sample size considerations, and outcomes) to test the two-morning-90-minute-blocks vs afternoon-heavy schedule comparison? Please include citations for key assumptions. L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.visible_text: Lumen + New thread TODAY Deep work scheduling literature EV battery recycling policy in Norway Trace prevalence of seal influenza H10N7 LAST 7 DAYS Comparative grad-school stipends in CS Microclimate effects of urban rooftop gardens Late-Holocene shoreline shifts, NW Europe Why does ringing happen in step responses EARLIER Survey: open-source funding models 2024 Caffeine half-life in slow metabolizers Building codes vs wildfire defensible space PA Priya Anand Researcher · Pro Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you propose a concrete study design (randomization, sample size considerations, and outcomes) to test the two-morning-90-minute-blocks vs afternoon-heavy schedule comparison? Please include citations for key assumptions. L Thinking out loud while I assemble sources… Here's a first pass. The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." Can you propose a concrete study design (randomization, sample size considerations, and outcomes) to test the two-morning-90-minute-blocks vs afternoon-heavy schedule comparison? The most directly relevant body of work is the chronotype × intervention literature; I'll prioritize that and bring in a couple of negative results to keep the picture honest. observation.visible_text: Deep work scheduling literature Share thread Export as PDF Mode: Balanced Mode: Quick scan Mode: Deep dive Mode: Compare arguments Hi — I'm planning a 6-week study on whether "two 90-minute deep-work blocks before noon" actually outperform afternoon-heavy schedules for software engineers. What does the existing literature say about this? L Short version: there's strong general support for protected morning blocks in attention-heavy work, but the specific comparison you're describing — two 90-minute blocks before noon vs. afternoon-heavy — has thin direct evidence and a lot of confounded chronotype work nearby. Here's how the field breaks down. Cognitive performance peaks vary by chronotype. Roughly 30% of working adults are "owls," for whom afternoon blocks aren't a deficit [1]. Pre-noon-heavy schedules show their largest effect for morning and intermediate types [2]. Block length matters more than block start time. The 90-min figure traces back to Kleitman's basic-rest-activity-cycle work and Ericsson's deliberate-practice studies; both argue for ~90-minute bouts, but neither pins them to morning [3]. The strongest field study I can find is Newport & Hempel's 2022 review of 11 industry interventions; protected blocks improved task completion by 18–32% regardless of time of day [4]. If you want a cleanly testable design, I'd recommend isolating "morning-loading" from "block protection" — otherwise any effect will be confounded. I can sketch a 2×2 protocol if you'd like. Yes please, sketch the 2×2. And how would you measure "deep work" output beyond self-report? L Sketch of a within-subjects 2×2 design (each engineer rotates through all four conditions, two weeks each): Morning-loaded Afternoon-loaded Protected blocks A: 2×90 min, 9–12 B: 2×90 min, 1–4 Unprotected (control) C: Schedule yourself, mornings D: Schedule yourself, afternoons For output measures beyond self-report, you've got three credible options: Code-event telemetry — merged-PR count, mean time from "first edit" to "first commit," IDE focus-session length. Drawbacks: noisy at the daily level [5]. Peer-rated weekly delivery scores — bias-adjusted Likert from one rotating reviewer, blinded to condition [6]. Cognitive bandwidth probes — n-back at 4 PM, ostensibly unrelated but predictive of after-work fatigue [7]. The cleanest single measure is probably "Total focus-session minutes per workday" measured by IDE plugin — it sidesteps self-report and is easy to log. Got it — give me one or two sentences I could put in the IRB proposal explaining why I'm not measuring "lines of code." L "Lines of code is a poor proxy for engineering output because it incentivizes verbosity and weakly correlates with task completion or code quality [8]. This study therefore measures protected focus-session minutes (from IDE telemetry) and bias-adjusted peer-rated weekly delivery, neither of which rewards code volume." 📎 Balanced Quick scan Deep dive Ask Follow-up questions Lumen suggests Find papers since 2020 directly comparing the two schedules Power analysis for 24 engineers × 2 weeks Surface negative results: where mornings didn't help Walk me through pre-registering on OSF Sources 8 Sort: Relevance Sort: Date Sort: Cited in this answer All Papers Books Web Preprints N Chronotype distribution in working adults — a meta-analysis Nature Sci Reports · 2021 · Olszewski et al. 0.88 "...approximately 31% of respondents in industrialized settings scored as evening-type or strongly evening-type, with mean peak alertness occurring after 14:00."
